To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ice recrystALLization inhibition activity of synthetic polymers is dependent on the molecular structure and the molecular mechanism.

(1) there is a wide variation in the ice recrystalization inhibition activities of different materials, (2) the mechanism of action can be either ice binding or the formation of a surface-active layer, and (3) the mechanism of ice binding can be either through a specific binding site or a nonspecific binding interaction, which can be either hydrophobic or electrostatic.

the IRI of antifreeze protein and antifreeze protein mimics are a continuum, and that the mechanism of activity is likely to be a combination of ice binding and/or amphiphilicity, depending on the material.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and development of synthetic macromolecules that mimic the ice recrystalling inhibition activity of natural antifreeze proteins.
the development of new materials with IRI activity, and this review article aims to provide a guide for others to see whether their materials are active or not.

the synthesis of new materials which are active at low concentrations and which can be produced in bulk quantities, with an aim to understand the molecular mechanisms which underpin their ice binding activity and to develop new materials with improved properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IRI activity of a material depends on the mechanism of action, the concentration of the material in the aqueous phase, the temperature, and the size and shape of the ice crystals.
a new polymer with IRI activity is active if it is more effective at IRI than poly(vinylpyrrolidone) or poly(ethylene glycol) at a concentration below 0.1 wt % in aqueous solution.
the IRI of a material can only be defined in terms of the conditions of measurement, which include the ice crystal size and the temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no “magic bullet” to mimic IRI and that a range of different materials with different properties will be required to address different problems.

the most active materials are likely to be amphiphilic, with the most active being those with the highest degree of amphiphilicity, and those which bind to ice are likely to be more active than those which do not.
a new polymer is “active” if its limiting concentration for ice growth is less than 0.1 wt % and the mechanism is likely to be ice binding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is not a single mechanism for IRI and that there are a number of ways in which a polymer can be “active” in this respect.

the IRI activity of materials can be compared and assigned into classes based upon the limiting concentration for ice growth and the mechanism of IRI, which can be used to guide the design of new materials.
there is a wide range of materials that can be considered to be “active” and there is a continuum of activity, rather than an all-or-nothing property.
